alt: An artificial neuron: inputs x1 to xn are multiplied by weights w1 to wn, added with a bias b in a summation unit (x times w plus b), passed through an activation function f(), and give the output y.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A neural network with an input layer x1 to xn, hidden layers and an output layer y1 to ym. Every input neuron connects to every hidden neuron, and every hidden neuron to every output neuron.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A table comparing a biological neuron with an artificial neuron on found in, structure, signal type, learning method, speed and real versus model.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Perceptron structure: inputs x1 to x4 and a bias b go into a summation circle, then an activation (step) box gives the output y. A simpler sketch shows the same as one circle called the neuron.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Example calculation of a perceptron with weights 0.5, 0.4, 0.6, 0.3, bias minus 1 and inputs 1, 1, 0.9, 0.8. Net equals 0.5 plus 0.4 plus 0.54 plus 0.24 minus 1, which is 0.68. Since 0.68 is at least 0, y is 1.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Perceptron for the AND gate: inputs x1 and x2 with weights 1 and 1, bias 0, a summation and a threshold theta equal to 2 in one circle, and output y.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Truth table of the AND perceptron. Sum is x1 times 1 plus x2 times 1: the sums 0, 1, 1, 2 give outputs 0, 0, 0, 1 because only 2 reaches the threshold 2.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: AND gate truth table, its four data points on an x1 versus x2 plot (only the point 1,1 is class 1) and a straight line that separates the classes. AND is linearly separable.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Why a single-layer perceptron fails on XOR: three different straight lines are tried on the four XOR points and one point is always on the wrong side, so XOR is not linearly separable.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Historical significance: 1958 Rosenblatt invents the perceptron; 1969 Minsky and Papert prove single-layer perceptrons cannot solve XOR and the AI winter begins; 1986 Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams introduce backpropagation for multi-layer networks and XOR becomes solvable.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: What a multi-layer perceptron is: a network with more than one layer, with an input layer, hidden layers and an output layer, each neuron connected to all neurons in the next layer, and why it is needed for complex and non-linear problems.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A 2-2-1 network for XOR: inputs x1 and x2, a hidden layer of two neurons with biases b1 and b2, and one output neuron with bias b3. Hidden neurons learn useful combinations of inputs and the output neuron gives the XOR result.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Decision boundary for XOR: a single perceptron draws one line and cannot separate the XOR points, while an MLP with a hidden layer draws a closed region that separates them.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: MLP architecture 2-2-1 for XOR with named weights: w11, w12, w21 and w22 from the inputs to hidden neurons h1 and h2, biases b1 and b2, weights w31 and w32 to the output Y, and bias b3.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A feedforward network with input, hidden and output layers. Information flows only forward. The legend names the input values, the hidden units (apply weights and activation) and the final output.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How a feedforward network works in six steps: input is given, inputs are multiplied with weights, bias is added, activation function is applied, output is passed to the next layer, final output is produced. For each neuron z equals the sum of w times x plus b and a equals f of z.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: More hidden layers: networks with 1, 2 and 3 or more hidden layers and the decision boundaries they draw, which get more complex with more layers.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Hierarchical feature learning: low-level input features go to the first hidden layer (edges), the second (shapes), the third (objects) and then the output decision, car or not car.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A deep network where the visible layer holds input pixels, the first hidden layer finds edges, the second corners and contours, the third object parts, and the output says car, person or animal. Beside it, the brain regions V1 and V2 do the same job.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: The universal approximation theorem: a feedforward network with a single hidden layer holding a finite number of neurons and a non-linear activation can approximate any continuous function on a compact subset of R^n to any desired accuracy.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Delta learning rule: delta w equals eta times (t minus y) times x, where eta is the learning rate, t the target output, y the actual output and x the input. It is used to reduce error and improve learning.
author: Deep Learning faculty
